### On fines, waiting lists and the quiet radicalism of lending.
My local branch library stopped charging late fines in 2021. Nobody made a speech about it. A laminated sign appeared by the returns slot, and the jar of coins that used to sit next to the date stamp quietly disappeared. Within a year, the librarians told me, the number of lapsed members coming back had nearly doubled.1
I have been thinking about that sign ever since, because it says something about how rare it has become to be offered a thing with no strings attached. Almost every other service in my life wants a subscription, an account, an email address or at least my attention. The library wants me to bring the book back when I am done with it.
## The waiting list
The most popular novel in my borough last year had a waiting list of four hundred and twelve people. I was number two hundred and something. It took five months to reach me, and when it did I read it in a weekend, partly because I knew a stranger was waiting behind me. There is a kind of civic feeling in that, a sense of being one link in a long chain of readers.
![Shelves of returned books on a trolley](https://substackcdn.example/image/fetch/w_1456,c_limit,f_auto/shelves.jpeg)
## What lending asks of us
Lending asks for trust in both directions. The library trusts me to return the book, and I trust that the book will be there, in roughly the condition I left it, for the next person. When fines were abolished, the library was simply making that trust explicit. The fines had never really paid for anything; the same report noted they cost more to collect than they brought in.
None of this is an argument against paying writers. I pay for several newsletters, including some I rarely read, because I want them to exist. It is an argument for keeping at least one door in the city that opens without a card reader.
1
The figure comes from the borough's own annual report, which is more readable than you might expect.
